title: Conversational stub app runway and checkpoints (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft for a compact developer-facing quickstart that uses a minimal conversational 'stub' app as the canonical way to teach the SDK, CLI, and Console integration. Goal is a 10–20 minute developer flow that demonstrates: auth, simple chat, streaming response, function/tool call, and telemetry (latency/cost/usage).

Audience:
- New engineers trying Redwood SDK for the first time (internal and external)
- Solutions engineers running live demos
- Docs + tutorial writers who want a reproducible app to reference

High-level constraints / design principles:
- Minimal surface area: one small Node or Python app, single env var for API key, one command to run in dev mode.
- Fail-safe by default: local fallbacks to a tiny deterministic stub LLM for offline demos.
- Observable: emits the same telemetry we show in Console (latency, token cost estimate, model id, route id).
- Reusable building blocks: CLI scaffolding, example prompt templates, and a tiny function-call example that calls a stub 'calendar' or 'vector search' service.

Quickstart skeleton (developer copy-paste):
1) git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/stub-convo-app
2) cp .env.example .env && export REDWOOD_API_KEY=pk_test_xxx
3) npm install (or pip install -r requirements.txt)
4) npm run dev (or python -m stub_app.main)
5) Open http://localhost:3000 and type a question.

What the quickstart demonstrates (explicit checkpoints):
- Checkpoint 1: Auth and basic roundtrip (server logs show successful token validation).
- Checkpoint 2: Streaming UI receives tokens in <200ms for small prompts (approx).
- Checkpoint 3: Function call path: user asks to 'schedule meeting' and app shows structured func payload + stub calendar response.
- Checkpoint 4: Telemetry events created (sdk.request.start, sdk.request.end, sdk.cache.hit/miss).
- Checkpoint 5: Local fallback triggers cleanly when API key missing (graceful UI message, returns canned response).

Developer-facing script examples (kept intentionally short):
- Node (server snippet):
  const Redwood = require('@redwood/inference-sdk');
  const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
  // simple chat call (streaming)
  client.chat.stream({ model: 'compat/gpt-small', messages: [...] })
    .on('token', tok => ws.send(tok))
    .on('done', () => console.log('done'));

- Python (sync example):
  from redwood import RedwoodClient
  c = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
  resp = c.chat.create(model='compat/gpt-small', messages=[...])
  print(resp.choices[0].message.content)

Smoke test checklist (what to validate in CI or dev run):
- App boots with no API key and serves fallback page (exit code 0).
- App boots with API key and returns 200 for /health and /metrics endpoints.
- Example chat flow completes within 2s for trivial prompt on local dev machine.
- Function-call example returns expected JSON schema (fields: name, start, end, status).
- Telemetry events captured and available on /metrics or printed to stdout in debug mode.

Telemetry and observability mapping (what we want to instrument here):
- sdk.request.start / sdk.request.end (with model, route, seq_len, tokens_in/tokens_out)
- sdk.stream.token (for measuring time-to-first-token and throughput)
- sdk.cache.hit/miss (if local prefix cache used for demo prompts)
- app.demo.step (custom events for Checkpoint 1..5)
- Export examples: console log lines + Prometheus-style /metrics endpoint for demos

Acceptance criteria for landing this quickstart in docs:
- Single-file quickstart (README) that reproduces the flow in under 20 minutes on Mac/Linux.
- Tests: basic smoke test script that runs in CI (GitHub Actions) with env var toggles for offline/local.
- PR with sample telemetry wired to a demo dashboard (Console link) and example logs attached.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Which model should we pick as the 'demo default'? (compat/gpt-small vs curated 1.0). Need perf baseline. @Marco to run perf sweep (Linear: SDK-412).
- Should the local fallback be a tiny on-device model (llama.cpp) or purely canned responses? Tradeoffs: reproducibility vs infra complexity. Proposal: canned deterministic stub first, upgrade later.
- Function-call surface: how far to go (one example vs multiple)? Start with one calendar-like function and a vector-search placeholder.
- Metrics: do we push demo telemetry to a tenant-specific sandbox or only show locally? Security/PII considerations.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (this doc): prototype + team review (2 weeks)
- Phase 1: basic quickstart + CI smoke tests + docs page (3 weeks)
- Phase 2: demo dashboard + observability wiring + guided Console tour (2 weeks)
- Phase 3: expand to Python + Go + mobile snippets (cross-language) (4 weeks)

Dependencies and blockers:
- small perf run to choose demo model (eng-serving-runtime)
- a docs engineer to author canonical README and landing page (developer-experience)
- agreement with Security on demo telemetry retention and sanitized sample data

Notes to self / rough action items:
- Build minimal GH Action: run smoke script in both offline and online modes.
- Add a unit test asserting telemetry event names and payload shape.
- Sketch a 'guided tour' overlay for Console that ties to the sample app (product + console-and-rollouts).
- Record a 3 minute internal screencast for Sales and Solutions engineers.

References / links to related work:
- existing SDK quickstarts (review list in DE Playbook)
- PR: stub-convo-app/pull/78 (initial scaffolding)
- Linear: SDK-412 (perf sweep), SDK-433 (telemetry schema)

If you are reviewing this doc: please comment on the 'fallback' approach and on the preferred default model. If nothing else, thumbs-up the Phase 0 plan and I will open the GH Action PR.

Owner: Aisha Patel
Last notes: keep the quickstart small and surgical—this will be our 'first app' in many demos, so friction matters more than perfect fidelity.
